title: I allocated $3B to quant hedge funds for years. Now I'm building one from scratch with AI tools, live, right now -- working on Portfolio Management Software tonight
author: stoaphil
selftext:
# building portfolio management software to make cool visuals for stream watchers tonight

Some background: several years ago I was head PM at an allocator, picking and monitoring mostly quantitative hedge funds with about $3B under management. I'm a CFA charterholder. I've sat through hundreds of quant manager pitches, so I know what the good ones look like, and what gets hand-waved.

Now I'm testing how far one person with AI coding tools can get building a real systematic fund: data pipeline, signal research, backtesting that doesn't lie, risk and portfolio construction. No course, nothing to sell. I'm building it on stream and narrating how an allocator would pick it apart.

Even the stream itself is run by an AI agent (it runs OBS, health checks and the recording), which is its own rabbit hole.

  
Working on portfolio management software tonight

Live now:  
Twitch: [twitch.tv/sudomyshkin](http://twitch.tv/sudomyshkin)  
YouTube: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ihXW4-dbDaw](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ihXW4-dbDaw)

Questions welcome in chat. Not investment advice, not raising money, just building in public.

comments.author: Brilliant_Potato4158
comments.body: you were a cog in a machine, good luck recreating the entire machine

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: Given the $3B allocator background, I’d be interested in the first visual you consider decision-useful rather than merely stream-friendly. Will the portfolio software show marginal contribution to risk and factor exposure alongside P&L, then let you attribute a drawdown to signal decay, sizing, or correlation shifts? That would also be a revealing test of the AI coding workflow: whether it preserves point-in-time positions and covariance inputs well enough to reconstruct what the PM could actually have known on each date.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the allocator angle is what makes this worth watching. from the other side of that table the first question was never the headline number, it was how many versions got tried before this one. one person with AI tools can run 200 variants in an afternoon and only show you the survivor.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: An allocator's view of what gets hand-waved in pitches is a useful lens for this. A segment I'd find valuable is a pre-registered research log on stream: write the hypothesis, the data period and the pass criteria before running anything, then show the trial count at the end so viewers can see how many ideas it took to find one that worked. For the "backtesting that doesn't lie" part, showing point-in-time data handling (publish dates, restatements, delisted names) would be a good thing to demonstrate live, and Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for earnings and macro releases) is one example of a source built around that. Good luck with the stream.
